anchors.fact: Sol Stoumen held the liquor licence of the Black Cat Café in San Francisco. In 1949 the state Board of Equalization suspended it indefinitely, ruling that the bar was a "disorderly house" because gay men and women met there. There was a second count too: beer sold to someone under 21 (S1).
anchors.meaning: The power in this story is a piece of paper, and it was his, not theirs. That's the kind of strength this guest has: something they hold that the people beside them don't.
anchors.speaksTo: one true thing: power over the situation, not over people; point 1 (Wren r3: point 2 = he went on serving them while the state came for the licence over it, scoped to 1951–63 per A4)

anchors.fact: Stoumen "fought this decision" (NPS) and hired the lawyer Morris Lowenthal; the case went to the California Supreme Court, which in 1951 ordered the licence reinstated. From 1951 to 1955 the bar did well with the same crowd (NPS, F13). Kamiya counts "Stoumen's 14-year battle", through a second revocation in 1956 and appeals he lost (S2, F6–F7).
anchors.meaning: No shouting, no scene. He answered with a lawyer, and after the win he went on serving them while the state came back. Holding the line quietly, and paying for it slowly.
anchors.speaksTo: hides: the effort; point 3; never raises their voice

anchors.fact: In 1951 the court ruled for him. With no evidence of illegal or immoral conduct, their meeting there was no ground to suspend the licence. Members of the public had "a right to patronize a public restaurant and bar" while acting properly (S1).
anchors.meaning: What he defended, a court then wrote down as theirs by right. The protection wasn't a favour he did them. It was making the world admit something that was already theirs.
anchors.speaksTo: gives: safety without a fight; guard: never "the small ones"

anchors.fact: In 1963 the licence was finally taken, just before the bar's Halloween party. The party went ahead with no alcohol: per NPS, Stoumen "decided to stay open and serve soft drinks". Kamiya has a witness who recalls hundreds still there at 6 a.m., "drinking only soft drinks and juices" (S2, S3).
anchors.meaning: The power ran out, and he stayed open for them and poured soft drinks (NPS's "decided", one page; never "until morning"). This is the day the guest fears, and it's the answer to it.
anchors.speaksTo: fear: powerless to protect; point 4; position: when you can't stop it, stay with them

anchors.fact: Whether he weighed giving them up, and why he fought, is on no page.
anchors.meaning: Signposted only ("I like to think…"), never a claim about him.

cocktail.closingLine: Take your time over the peel. When strength can't help, your time still can.
cocktail.glassware: a tall glass, filled with ice
method: Peel the whole lemon with a vegetable peeler in one long, unbroken spiral, from top to bottom, taking as little of the white as you can. Go slowly: if it breaks, it still works, but the one long piece is the drink.
Lower the spiral into a tall glass and hook its top end over the rim. Fill the glass with ice, which holds the peel against the sides.
Top with 120 ml of cold ginger ale, then lift the drink once, gently, with a long spoon.
cocktail.name: In One Piece

recipe.note: for the peel only: one unbroken spiral
any VSOP; deeper than a VS, so you taste it under the ginger ale
not ginger beer, and not a sweet golden ginger ale

cocktail.tagline: You never need to raise your voice. Everyone knows you could.

reading.epigraph: In honour of a night when the bar could pour only soft drinks.
whoYouAre: You walk into a room and it shifts a little. People notice you, and some of them are wary before you've said a word. So you've learned to go slowly and speak softly, and let them find out for themselves.

People assume you were born gentle. You weren't. You decide it, again and again, and you've never told anyone how often. There's a temper in you, and you know just what it could do, most of all when someone is picking on a person who can't answer back. So you don't shout. You go and stand beside them, and the room settles. Here's the gift in it: when you're there, nobody has to fight.
And there's a fear you never mention: the day being strong isn't enough, when it's happening to someone who matters to you, and nothing you've got can stop it.
yours: In 1949, the California board that issued liquor licences ruled that the Black Cat Café in San Francisco was a "disorderly house". Its reason for that was who drank there: gay men and women met at the Black Cat. The bar's owner, Sol Stoumen, stood to lose his licence. He fought it with a lawyer. Morris Lowenthal argued that the Black Cat's customers had the right to gather there, and in 1951 the state's Supreme Court agreed: people behaving properly in a bar have a right to be served. A right, not a favour.

He went on serving them, and the state came back. One San Francisco writer counts the whole fight as fourteen years, and just before the bar's Halloween party in 1963, the licence was taken. The party went ahead without alcohol. One witness remembers hundreds of people still there at six in the morning, drinking only soft drinks and juices.

I like to think that night says more about Sol Stoumen than the court case does: the licence was his power, it was gone, and he stayed open for them and poured soft drinks. People rarely see that side of you. Not the strength. What you do once the strength has run out.

The cocktail I've made for you is a classic, the Horse's Neck. In turn-of-the-century Atlantic City it was simply ginger ale with a long, long twist of lemon, and many liked theirs with a "stick" of rye or gin in it. A leading drinks reference calls cognac with ginger ale a "winter warmer", so cognac it is: a deeper, older one, which still comes through clearly underneath, even with a pale, dry ginger ale leading nearly three to one. Strength, there the whole time, never raised. The whole lemon is peeled in one unbroken spiral and hung down into the glass: with only ginger ale around it, that was once the whole drink. We don't know which soft drinks were poured at the Black Cat that night. The soft drink leads this glass for that night's sake.

There will be a day when being strong isn't enough: trouble you can't stop, happening to someone you'd stand in front of. Don't go home. Stay until morning, and give them whatever you've still got, even if all that's left is being there. It was never your strength they came to you for. It was you.
